name: Alopecia Areata
description: An autoimmune condition causing patchy, non-scarring hair loss that can occur at any age.
whatIsIt: Alopecia areata is a common cause of patchy hair loss characterised by well-demarcated, shiny patches of non-scarring hair loss. Short, exclamation-mark hairs may be visible at the periphery of the affected area.
causedBy: Autoimmune disease directed at the hair follicles
Family history of autoimmune disease
Can occur at any age
symptoms: Well-demarcated shiny patches of hair loss
Short exclamation-mark hairs at the edge of the lesion
Generally asymptomatic (no pain or itching)
treatments: GP can prescribe steroids (injected or applied directly as creams or liquids) to affected areas
Steroids suppress the immune cells attacking hair follicles, allowing hair to regrow
keyFacts: Unpredictable course — normally resolves over time
Nail involvement (pitting) may be present
Non-scarring — follicles are not permanently damaged
Can occur at any age

name: Female Pattern Hair Loss
description: A genetically driven condition causing progressive thinning across the mid-frontal scalp, often worsened by hormonal changes.
whatIsIt: Female pattern hair loss (FPHL) generally presents as a loss of hair volume to the mid-frontal scalp. The parting appears to be getting wider and hair overall feels thinner. It is also known as androgenetic alopecia in women.
causedBy: Genetically driven — involves activation of hair follicle androgen receptors
Miniaturisation of the hair follicle resulting in progressive hair loss
Caused by a combination of hormones, ageing and genetics
May be exacerbated by low ferritin (iron) levels or thyroid dysfunction
symptoms: Widening of the hair parting
Thinning around the parting area
Reduced volume in a ponytail
Overall thinning of hair throughout the head
Psychological impact — low self-esteem
treatments: Minoxidil (topical treatment to slow hair loss)
Topical steroids from GP
Light therapy
Wigs or hair transplants
keyFacts: There is no cure for FPHL
Hair loss is not constant — accelerated phases of 3–6 months are followed by periods of stability lasting 6–18 months
Without medication, it tends to progress in severity over decades

name: Frontal Fibrosing Alopecia
description: A scarring form of hair loss affecting the front and sides of the scalp, where destroyed follicles cannot regrow.
whatIsIt: Frontal fibrosing alopecia (FFA) causes hair loss on the front and sides of the scalp. It is a scarring alopecia, meaning the hair follicles are destroyed and replaced by scar tissue. Hair loss may also affect the eyebrows, eyelashes and other body parts.
causedBy: An autoimmune reaction targeting hair follicles
Genetics may play a role
Hormonal factors may contribute
symptoms: Progressive hair loss on the front and sides of the scalp
Loss of eyebrows, eyelashes and body hair
Rash along the hairline in some cases
Itchy or painful scalp in some cases
treatments: Referral to GP for topical steroid cream or ointment
Steroid injections may be an option in some cases
Treatment aims to prevent further follicle destruction but cannot regrow hair already lost
keyFacts: Scarring alopecia — destroyed follicles cannot regrow
Hair that has been lost will not grow back
Early treatment is important to prevent further progression

name: Male Pattern Hair Loss
description: The most common form of hair loss in men, driven by genetic and hormonal factors causing gradual thinning at the temples and crown.
whatIsIt: Male pattern hair loss (MPHL), also known as androgenetic alopecia, presents as hair loss at the temples or crown of the head. Hairlines may recede to form an "M" shape, or a single spot of baldness may develop at the crown.
causedBy: Combination of genetic and hormonal factors
DHT (Dihydrotestosterone) causes changes in hair follicles on the scalp
Affected follicles produce progressively smaller, shorter and lighter hairs until they stop producing hair entirely
Inherited from either or both parents
symptoms: Hair loss at the temples or crown of the head
Receding hairline forming an "M" shape
Awareness of thinning after puberty — usually no physical symptoms on the scalp
Psychological impact — low self-esteem, depression and feelings of unattractiveness
treatments: Minoxidil (topical treatment — slows hair loss if taken continuously)
Finasteride (oral medication — reduces levels of DHT)
Wigs or hair pieces
Micro-pigmentation
Hair transplants
keyFacts: There is no cure
Tends to progress very slowly over several years to decades
Early onset may lead to quicker progression
Inherited from either or both parents

name: Traction Alopecia
description: Hair loss caused by repeated or constant pulling on the hair, often from tight hairstyling techniques.
whatIsIt: Traction alopecia is hair loss resulting from repeated or constant pulling on the hair. It typically appears as areas of hair loss to the front and sides of the scalp, punctuated with broken hairs. The pulling force is usually from hairstyling techniques such as tight ponytails, braids, cornrows or dreadlocks.
causedBy: Repeated or constant pulling on the hair from tight hairstyling
Tight ponytails exerting extreme pulling force on the hair and scalp
Afro-Caribbean styling techniques — braids, cornrows, dreadlocks
symptoms: Areas of hair loss, often at the front and sides of the scalp
Broken hairs in the affected area
Inflammation, soreness, stinging or itchiness of the scalp
treatments: Stop tight hairstyles immediately
Anti-biotic from GP if the area is inflamed
Early intervention gives the best chance of recovery
keyFacts: Often not reversible if left untreated
If treated quickly, follicles can recover and hair will grow back normally
Continued traction causes inflammation that affects stem cells, creating scarring and permanent hair loss

name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
description: A common, recurring scalp condition causing red, yellowy, flaky scales, often linked to yeast, genetics and stress.
whatIsIt: Seborrheic dermatitis is a common inflammatory skin condition that appears on the scalp as red, yellowy, flaky scales. It can also affect the nasal folds, eyebrows, armpits and groin. It is a long-term, recurring condition that can be managed but not cured.
causedBy: Genetic predisposition
Yeast infection (Malassezia)
Stress-related triggers
Temperature change — can be worse in winter
symptoms: Red, yellowy, flaky scales on the scalp
Inflammation and soreness
May also appear on nasal folds, eyebrows, armpits and groin
treatments: Medicated anti-dandruff shampoo from the pharmacy
Descaling preparation may be needed first (coconut oil or salicylic acid)
Topical steroid cream from GP if needed
keyFacts: Can be managed but is a long-term, recurring condition
Often worse in winter months
Also known as seborrheic eczema

name: Telogen Effluvium
description: Excessive, sudden hair shedding triggered by an underlying internal condition such as illness, hormonal change or nutritional deficiency.
whatIsIt: Telogen effluvium is a sudden loss of hair due to various internal factors, resulting in excessive hair shedding. It is a clinical sign that signals the existence of an underlying condition rather than a disease in itself. In rare cases it may also cause hair loss on the pubic region or eyebrows.
causedBy: Post-partum hair loss
Febrile illness
Blood loss
Post-operative responses
Endocrine disorders
Drugs and medication
Metabolic and nutritional disorders
symptoms: Sudden excessive hair shedding
Noticeable increase in hair fall during washing or brushing
Generally asymptomatic on the scalp
In rare cases, hair loss on the pubic region or eyebrows
treatments: Treatment is directed at the underlying cause
Identifying and addressing the trigger condition is key to recovery
keyFacts: Once the underlying cause is treated, prognosis is normally good and hair growth resumes
Not a disease itself — it signals an underlying condition
Hair shedding is typically temporary

name: Trichotillosis
description: A self-inflicted hair condition caused by repeated pulling, twisting or rubbing of the hair, often linked to stress and compulsive behaviour.
whatIsIt: Trichotillosis (also referred to as trichotillomania) is a self-inflicted condition that arises from repeated pulling, twisting or rubbing of strands of hair. The most common site of hair loss is the scalp, where hair looks twisted and fragmented. It may also affect eyelashes and eyebrows.
causedBy: Stress-related and compulsive behaviour
Psychological factors — especially in children
Linked to stress reduction, emotional regulation and sensory stimulation
symptoms: Twisted and fragmented hair on the scalp
Patchy hair loss from repeated pulling
Hair loss to eyelashes and eyebrows
Sense of pleasure or relief after hair is pulled
treatments: Seeking treatment for depression, anxiety or poor self-image
Psychological or behavioural therapy to address underlying triggers
keyFacts: For most people, the hair pulling ends within 12 months
For others, it can be a lifelong disorder
Most common in children and young adults

name: Irritant Contact Dermatitis
description: A temporary skin reaction on the scalp caused by exposure to chemicals or harmful substances, commonly seen in hairdressers.
whatIsIt: Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) is a reaction that takes place when the skin barrier is damaged after exposure to a chemical or harmful substance. The most common occurrence of ICD is on the scalp and hands of people who frequently use detergents and water, often through their work (such as hairdressers).
causedBy: Lengthy exposure to detergents or water removes the natural oils of the outer skin layers, causing irritation
Chemical agents penetrating the protective outer layers of the skin trigger an inflammatory response
The body reacts by attempting to neutralise the invading agent and repair damage
symptoms: Soreness, redness and inflammation of the affected area
Cracked or dry skin
Skin may be weeping with fluid in some areas
treatments: Emollient cream from the pharmacy
Topical corticosteroid from GP if extremely inflamed
Avoid exposure to the damaging substance
keyFacts: ICD is a temporary skin reaction
Usually calms when exposure to the damaging substance is avoided
Most common in people who frequently handle detergents and water

name: Allergic Contact Dermatitis
description: A type 4 allergic skin reaction causing itchy, red, blistered patches, triggered by repeated exposure to an allergen.
whatIsIt: Allergic contact dermatitis is an allergic skin reaction that occurs 12–72 hours after exposure to an allergen. It presents as redness, heat, swelling and pain on the scalp or affected area. It is classified as a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction.
causedBy: Repeated exposure to small doses of an allergen
Overreaction of the body's autoimmune system
Many different allergens can trigger this condition
symptoms: Redness, heat, swelling and pain
Patches of skin that are itchy, red and blistered
Reaction occurs 12–72 hours after exposure
Sun sensitivity may also be present
treatments: Avoid contact with the triggering substance
Hydrocortisone cream from GP or pharmacy
Antihistamine medication
Topical steroids if needed
keyFacts: Once the body is sensitised to an allergen, it is for life
Identifying and avoiding the allergen is the most important step
Reaction is delayed — appears 12–72 hours after exposure

name: Folliculitis
description: An infection causing inflammation of the hair follicles, resulting in itchiness, burning and redness. Easily treated and curable.
whatIsIt: Folliculitis is a skin condition in which hair follicles become inflamed, typically due to a bacterial infection. It can occur anywhere on hair-bearing skin, though it commonly affects the scalp.
causedBy: Bacterial infection of the hair follicle
Folliculitis decalvans (a more severe form)
Can occur on any hair-bearing skin
symptoms: Itchiness within the affected follicle
Burning sensation
Redness and inflammation around the follicle
treatments: GP referral for appropriate treatment
Antibiotics may be prescribed depending on severity
keyFacts: Very good prognosis — easily treated and curable
Can occur anywhere on hair-bearing skin
Early treatment prevents complications
